summary: Specifies the SIP P-Profile-Key private header, used in 3GPP IMS to give registrars and proxies the key of the profile matching the destination of a request. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5002 defines a SIP header for sharing a profile lookup key between proxies in a 3GPP IP Multimedia Subsystem. It avoids asking the user database to find the same wildcard match again.

questions: what is the sip p-profile-key header
what is a wildcarded public service identity
what does the i-cscf do with p-profile-key
what is the sip p profile key header
subtitle: A private SIP header that passes a profile lookup key between proxies in 3GPP IMS.

tldr.problem: Two proxies in 3GPP IMS may need the same user profile, and repeatedly searching wildcard identities can take time and work.
tldr.mechanism: The first proxy places the matching wildcarded identity in a P-Profile-Key header; the next proxy uses that value as its database lookup key.
tldr.outcome: The header is intended for trusted 3GPP IMS networks and has been updated by RFC 8217.

today: RFC 5002 is Informational and was updated by RFC 8217. Its text limits the header's intended use to trusted 3GPP IMS networks.

sections.title: Why Wildcard Lookups Can Repeat
sections.content:
In 3GPP IMS, several proxies handling one request may consult the same user database. A request to a Public Service Identity may match a Wildcarded Public Service Identity, which represents multiple service identities using a regular expression.

If the database must search its wildcard entries each time, two proxies can cause the same matching work to be repeated. The RFC describes this search as potentially expensive or time-consuming.
sections.plainLanguage: A request may fit a pattern that covers many service addresses. If two proxies ask the database about that request, it may have to find the same matching pattern twice.

sections.title: Passing the Matching Profile Key
sections.content:
The proposed solution is for the first proxy to obtain the matching wildcard identity from the user database and carry it in the SIP request. The next proxy can then query the database with that identity directly.

The RFC rejects storing every individual service identity with its matching wildcard as an undesirable alternative because the database would be harder to scale and manage.
sections.plainLanguage: The first proxy passes the matching pattern to the next proxy. The next proxy can use that pattern instead of searching for it again.

sections.title: The P-Profile-Key Header
sections.content:
The P-Profile-Key field contains the key that a proxy uses to query the user database for a profile. Its syntax permits a name-addr or addr-spec and optional generic parameters.

In the intended use, the value can be a Wildcarded Public Service Identity written as an Extended Regular Expression. The RFC's example uses a pattern for chatroom identities at example.com.
sections.plainLanguage: The header carries the identity pattern that matched the requested service. A proxy can use that value to find the corresponding profile.

sections.title: Where the Header Applies
sections.content:
The header is intended for 3GPP IMS. The I-CSCF inserts it into a SIP request and the S-CSCF removes it before routing the request onward. Both proxies share an administrative domain and a common view of the user database.

The RFC says that this arrangement is not typical of general Internet SIP, where multiple trusted proxies do not usually query the same user database. It therefore does not present the header as a general SIP feature.
sections.plainLanguage: The header is for two trusted proxies that share one user database. The receiving proxy removes the header before it sends the request onward.

sections.title: Integrity and Confidentiality
sections.content:
The RFC assumes that the proxies are trusted and that attackers cannot read or alter messages between them. It says the header must not be used where those assumptions do not hold.

The header needs integrity protection because an altered value could cause a different service profile to be applied. It also needs confidentiality because its contents reveal information about how services are organized in the domain.
sections.plainLanguage: Only trusted systems should handle this header. Protect it from changes and from being read by parties that should not learn how services are organized.
